title: Chapter 15. Of Other Laws of Nature
paragraphs: From the law of nature that obliges us to transfer to another any rights whose retention would hinder the peace of mankind, there follows a third law: that people keep the covenants they make. Without this, covenants are pointless — mere empty words — and since everyone's right to everything would still remain, we would still be in a state of war.

This law of nature is the fountain and origin of JUSTICE. Where no covenant has been made, no right has been transferred, and everyone has a right to everything — so no action can be unjust. But once a covenant is made, breaking it is unjust. And the definition of INJUSTICE is simply the failure to perform a covenant. Whatever is not unjust is just.

[Justice and property begin with the founding of a commonwealth.] But because covenants of mutual trust — where there's a fear that one side won't perform, as was said in the previous chapter — are invalid, the origin of justice is indeed in making covenants, yet there can be no actual injustice until the cause of that fear is removed. And that cannot be done while men remain in the natural condition of war. So before the words “just” and “unjust” can have any meaning, there must be some coercive power to compel people equally to keep their covenants — by threatening a punishment greater than the benefit they'd expect from breaking the covenant — and to secure the property that people acquire by mutual contract in exchange for the universal right they give up. No such power exists before a commonwealth is established. This can also be seen from the standard definition of justice given in the schools — that is, in scholastic philosophy: they say “Justice is the constant will to give every man his own.” So where there is no “own” — that is, no property — there is no injustice; and where no coercive power has been set up — that is, where there is no commonwealth — there is no property, since everyone has a right to everything. So where there is no commonwealth, nothing is unjust. The nature of justice, then, consists in keeping valid covenants — but covenants become valid only once a civil power exists that's strong enough to compel people to keep them. And that is also when property begins.

The fool has said in his heart that there's no such thing as justice — and sometimes he says it aloud too — seriously arguing that since every man's survival and contentment is his own responsibility, there's no reason he shouldn't do whatever he thinks will serve it; and therefore making or breaking, keeping or not keeping covenants isn't against reason when doing so benefits him. He doesn't deny that covenants exist, that they're sometimes broken and sometimes kept, or that breaking them can be called injustice and keeping them justice. But he asks whether injustice — once it has set aside the fear of God (for this same fool has also said in his heart that there is no God) — might not sometimes agree with the reason that tells every man to pursue his own good, particularly when it leads to a benefit great enough to let a man ignore not just other people's scorn and abuse but their power as well. The kingdom of God is taken by force — but what if it could be taken by unjust force? Would it be against reason to take it that way, if doing so couldn't possibly harm you? And if it isn't against reason, it isn't against justice either — or else justice shouldn't be considered good. Reasoning like this has let successful wickedness pass for virtue; and some people who condemn breaking one's word in every other case have allowed it when the prize is a kingdom. Even the pagans, who believed that Saturn was overthrown by his son Jupiter, still believed that this same Jupiter punished injustice — rather like a point of law in Coke's Commentary on Littleton, where he says that if the rightful heir to the crown is convicted of treason, the crown will still pass to him, and the conviction becomes void the instant it does. From cases like these, one might easily conclude that when the heir apparent to a kingdom kills the person holding it — even if that person is his own father — you can call it injustice or whatever else you like, but it can never be against reason, since all voluntary human actions aim at one's own benefit, and the most reasonable actions are the ones that best achieve their aim. This plausible-sounding argument is nevertheless false.

The question here isn't about mutual promises where neither side has any guarantee the other will perform — as when no civil power has been set up over the people making the promise, since such promises aren't really covenants at all. The real question concerns cases where one party has already performed, or where a power exists to make him perform: is it against reason — that is, against his own benefit — for the other party to perform or not? I say it is not against reason. To show this, consider first that when a man does something which, as far as anyone could foresee or calculate, tends toward his own destruction, the fact that some unforeseeable accident later turns it to his advantage doesn't make the act itself reasonable or wise. Second, in a state of war, where every man is an enemy to every other man for lack of a common power to keep them all in check, no one can hope to defend himself from destruction by his own strength or cleverness alone, without the help of allies — and everyone in an alliance expects the same protection from it that anyone else does. So a man who announces that he thinks it reasonable to betray those who help him can, by that same reasoning, expect no safety beyond what his own unaided strength can provide. He who breaks his covenant — and so declares that he thinks he may reasonably do so — cannot be admitted into any society formed for peace and mutual defense, except by the mistake of those who admit him; nor, once admitted, can he be kept there once that mistake is recognized. And a man cannot reasonably count on other people's mistakes as a means of keeping himself safe. So if he is left out of society, or thrown out of it, he perishes; and if he does live within society, it's only because of errors other men made that he couldn't have foreseen or relied on — which means his survival runs against the very reasoning that was supposed to secure it. In short, everyone who doesn't actively destroy him does so only out of ignorance of what's actually good for themselves.

As for the example of gaining heaven's secure and everlasting happiness by any means whatever — that argument is worthless, since there is only one way anyone can imagine reaching it, and that way is not breaking but keeping one's covenant.

And as for the other example — gaining sovereignty through rebellion — it's clear that even when it succeeds, success could not reasonably have been expected; the more likely outcome was the opposite. And because succeeding this way teaches others to try the same thing, attempting it is against reason. Justice, then — that is, keeping one's covenants — is a rule of reason that forbids us from doing anything destructive to our own life, and is therefore a law of nature.

Some go further still, and hold that the law of nature isn't really about the rules that preserve a man's life on earth, but about reaching eternal happiness after death — to which, they think, breaking a covenant might sometimes contribute, and so be just and reasonable. (These are the people who think it a meritorious act to kill, depose, or rebel against the sovereign power set over them by their own consent.) But since there is no natural way of knowing what happens to a man after death — let alone what reward is given there for breaking one's word — and all we have is a belief based on what other people claim to know by supernatural revelation, or claim to have heard from others who knew others who knew it supernaturally, breaking one's word cannot be called a precept of reason or of nature.

Others accept that keeping one's word is a law of nature but still make exceptions for certain people — heretics, for instance, and those who habitually fail to keep their covenants with others. This too is against reason. For if some fault in a man were enough to release us from a covenant already made with him, that same fault ought, by the same reasoning, to have been enough to keep us from making the covenant in the first place.

The words “just” and “unjust” mean one thing when applied to men and another when applied to actions. Applied to men, they signify whether a person's character conforms to reason or not. Applied to actions, they signify whether a particular action — not a way of life in general — conforms to reason. A just man, then, is someone who takes every care he can that all his actions be just; an unjust man is someone who neglects to. In our language, such people are more often called righteous and unrighteous than just and unjust, though the meaning is the same. So a righteous man doesn't lose that title over one or a few unjust acts that come from sudden passion or a mistake about facts or people; and an unrighteous man doesn't lose his character on account of just actions he performs, or wrong actions he refrains from, out of fear — because in his case the will behind the act isn't shaped by justice but by whatever seems to benefit him at the time. What gives human actions the flavor of justice is a certain nobility or generosity of spirit (rarely found) by which a man disdains to owe the comforts of his life to fraud or broken promises. This is the justice of character that people mean when they call justice a virtue and injustice a vice.
But the justice of actions makes men not just, but merely blameless; and the injustice of actions — also called injury — makes them merely guilty.

Again, injustice of character is the tendency or readiness to commit injury, and counts as injustice even before it results in any act, and without there needing to be any particular person wronged. But the injustice of an action — that is, an injury — requires a particular person to have been wronged: namely, the one to whom the covenant was made. So it often happens that one man receives the injury while another bears the damage. For instance, if a master orders his servant to give money to a stranger and the servant fails to do it, the injury is done to the master, whom the servant had earlier covenanted to obey; but the damage falls on the stranger, to whom the servant owed nothing, and whom he therefore could not have wronged. Likewise, within commonwealths, private citizens can forgive one another's debts, but not robberies or other acts of violence done against them — because withholding a debt injures only the person owed, while robbery and violence injure the commonwealth itself as a person.

Whatever is done to a man with his own consent, made known to the one who does it, is no injury to him. For if the one doing it hasn't given up his original right to act as he pleases through some prior covenant, there's no breach of covenant, and so no injury is done. And if he has given it up, then his expressed wish to have the thing done releases that covenant — so again, no injury is done.

Writers divide the justice of actions into commutative and distributive: the first, they say, follows arithmetical proportion — that is, equality of amount — the second geometrical proportion — that is, equality of ratio. Commutative justice they locate in the equal value of the things exchanged in a contract; distributive justice, in giving an equal benefit to men of equal merit — as though it were unjust to sell for more than you paid, or to give one man more than he deserves. But the value of anything contracted for is measured by what the parties to the contract want, and so the just value is whatever they're content to give. And merit — apart from the merit created by covenant, where performance on one side earns performance on the other, which falls under commutative, not distributive, justice — is not owed as a matter of justice at all; it is rewarded only as a matter of grace. So this distinction, understood the way it's usually explained, isn't correct. Properly speaking, commutative justice is the justice of a party to a contract — that is, keeping one's covenant in buying and selling, hiring out and hiring, lending and borrowing, exchanging, bartering, and other contractual dealings.

And distributive justice is the justice of an arbitrator — that is, the act of determining what is just. In this role, once trusted by the people who appointed him arbitrator, if he carries out that trust he is said to give each person his own; and that really is just distribution, and might loosely be called distributive justice, though it's more properly called equity — which is also a law of nature, as will be shown in its proper place.

Just as justice depends on a prior covenant, gratitude depends on a prior act of grace — that is, a prior free gift. This is the fourth law of nature, which can be stated as: “A man who receives a benefit from another purely out of grace should see to it that the giver has no reasonable cause to regret his goodwill.” For no one gives except with some intention of benefiting himself, since giving is voluntary, and the object of every voluntary act is, for everyone, his own good. If people saw that this would be frustrated, there would be no start to benevolence or trust, and consequently none to mutual help or to reconciliation between one man and another — so they would remain stuck in the condition of war, which goes against the first and fundamental law of nature commanding men to seek peace. Breaking this law is called ingratitude, and it bears the same relation to grace that injustice bears to obligation created by covenant.

A fifth law of nature is COMPLAISANCE — that is, “everyone should try to accommodate himself to the rest.” To understand this, consider that people's fitness for society varies according to their differing temperaments — much like the stones gathered for building a structure. A stone whose rough, irregular shape takes up more room than it fills, and whose hardness makes it hard to smooth down, gets in the way of the building and so is thrown aside by the builders as useless and troublesome. In the same way, a man whose difficult temperament makes him insist on keeping things that are unnecessary to himself but needed by others, and whose stubborn passions can't be corrected, ought to be left out or cast out of society as a burden to it. For since every man, both by right and by the necessity of his nature, is assumed to do everything he can to obtain what's necessary for his own survival, anyone who resists him over things that are merely superfluous is responsible for the resulting conflict, and so acts against the fundamental law of nature commanding people to seek peace. Those who observe this law may be called SOCIABLE (the Latins call them commodi); those who break it, stubborn, unsociable, peevish, intractable.

A sixth law of nature is this: “Given assurance about future conduct, a man ought to pardon the past offenses of those who, repenting, ask for it.” For pardon is nothing but the granting of peace. Peace granted to those who persist in hostility isn't really peace but fear; but refusing it to those who give assurance about their future conduct is a sign of hostility to peace, and so is against the law of nature.
[The seventh law: in taking revenge, men should look only to the future good.]

A seventh law is: “In taking revenge — that is, in repaying evil with evil — people should not look at how great the past wrong was, but at how great the good to come will be.” This forbids us from inflicting punishment for any purpose other than correcting the offender or setting an example for others. This law follows from the one just before it, which commands pardon once future security is assured. Besides, revenge that pays no regard to setting an example or to any future benefit is simply gloating over another's suffering, aimed at nothing (since an end is always something still to come); and gloating that aims at nothing is vainglory, and against reason. And to hurt someone without reason tends to bring on war, which is against the law of nature, and is commonly called cruelty.

And because every sign of hatred or contempt provokes conflict — so much so that most men would rather risk their lives than go unavenged — we may set down, as an eighth law of nature, this rule: “No man should declare hatred or contempt for another, by act, word, expression, or gesture.” Breaking this law is commonly called contumely — that is, open insult or scorn.

The question of who is the better man has no place in the condition of pure nature, where, as has already been shown, all men are equal. Whatever inequality exists now has been introduced by civil laws. I know that Aristotle, in the first book of his Politics, lays it down as a foundation of his theory that some men are by nature more fit to command — meaning the wiser sort, such as he considered himself to be on account of his philosophy — and others fit only to serve, meaning those with strong bodies but no philosophy like his. This treats the relation of master and servant as though it arose not from people's consent but from a difference in intelligence — which goes against both reason and experience. For very few people are foolish enough to prefer being governed by others to governing themselves; and when men who consider themselves wise try to force their will on people who have no confidence in their own wisdom, they don't always — or even often, or hardly ever — come out the winners. So if nature has in fact made men equal, that equality should be acknowledged; and even if nature has made men unequal, since men who consider themselves equal won't accept peace except on equal terms, that same equality must still be granted. And so, as the ninth law of nature, I set down this: “Every man should acknowledge every other man as his equal by nature.” Breaking this rule is called pride.

Another law follows from this one: “At the point of entering into peace, no man should claim for himself any right that he isn't willing to see granted to everyone else.” Just as it is necessary for everyone seeking peace to lay down certain natural rights — that is, to give up the freedom to do whatever they please — it is also necessary for human life to keep hold of some rights: the right to govern one's own body, to have access to air, water, and movement, to travel from place to place, and all the other things without which a person cannot live, or cannot live well. If, in making peace, men demand for themselves things they would refuse to grant to others, they violate the previous law requiring the acknowledgment of natural equality, and so also violate the law of nature. Those who observe this law we call modest; those who break it, arrogant. The Greeks call the violation of this law pleonexia — that is, wanting more than one's fair share.

Also, “if a man is entrusted to judge between one person and another,” it is a rule of the law of nature “that he deal equally between them.” Without that, disputes between people can be settled only by war. Anyone who judges with partiality does, as far as it's in his power, discourage people from using judges and arbitrators at all — and so, contrary to the fundamental law of nature, becomes a cause of war.

Observing this law — the equal distribution to each man of what reason says belongs to him — is called EQUITY, and, as I said before, distributive justice; violating it is called favoritism, or Prosopolepsia — that is, showing partiality toward particular persons.

From this follows another law: “Things that cannot be divided should be enjoyed in common, if possible — without limit, if the quantity allows it; otherwise in proportion to the number of people who have a right to it.” Otherwise the distribution would be unequal, and contrary to equity.

But there are some things that can neither be divided nor held in common. In that case, the law of nature that requires equity demands: “That the entire right — or, if the use can be alternated, the first possession — be decided by lot.” For equal distribution belongs to the law of nature, and no other means of achieving it can be conceived.

There are two kinds of lot: arbitrary and natural. An arbitrary lot is one agreed upon by the competitors. A natural lot is either primogeniture — which the Greeks call kleronomia, meaning “given by lot” — or first seizure.
And so, things that cannot be shared in common or divided ought to be granted to the first person who takes possession of them — and in some cases to the firstborn, as something acquired by lot.

It is also a law of nature that “all men who mediate for peace should be granted safe passage.” For the law that commands peace as an end also commands the means to it — negotiation — and the means to negotiation is safe passage.

And because, however willing people may be to observe these laws, questions can still arise about a man's action — first, whether it was done at all, and second, if it was done, whether it violated the law or not (the first kind of question being a question of fact, the second a question of right) — unless the parties to the dispute agree to abide by the judgment of a third party, they remain as far from peace as ever. This third party, to whose judgment they submit, is called an ARBITRATOR. And so it is a law of nature that “those in dispute should submit their claim to the judgment of an arbitrator.”

And since every man is presumed to act in his own interest in everything he does, no man is fit to be arbitrator in his own case. And even if he were perfectly fit, equity still requires equal benefit to each side — so if one party is allowed to be the judge, the other must be allowed the same; and so the dispute, meaning the cause of the war, remains, against the law of nature.
[The eighteenth law: no man should be judge who has in him a cause of bias.]

For the same reason, no man ought to be accepted as arbitrator in any case where greater profit, honor, or pleasure would plainly come to him from one side winning rather than the other. For in accepting the case he has, in effect, taken a bribe — even if an unavoidable one — and no one can be required to trust him. So here too the dispute, and the state of war, persists, against the law of nature.

And in a dispute over fact, since the judge has no more reason to believe one party than the other (assuming there is no other evidence), he must give credence to a third party — or to a third and a fourth, or more. Otherwise the question remains undecided and is left to be settled by force, against the law of nature.

These are the laws of nature that dictate peace as a means of preserving mankind in large numbers, and which alone concern the doctrine of civil society. There are other things that tend toward the destruction of particular individuals — such as drunkenness and every other form of excess — which could therefore also be counted among the things the law of nature forbids; but they don't need to be mentioned here, and aren't relevant enough to this discussion.

And although this deduction of the laws of nature may seem too subtle for most people to notice — since most are too busy earning a living, and the rest too careless to work it out — still, so that no one is left with an excuse, these laws have been condensed into a single easy formula, understandable even to the dullest mind: “Do not do to another what you would not want done to yourself.” This shows a man that, to learn the laws of nature, he needs do no more than this: when weighing other men's actions against his own and finding them too heavy, put them on the other side of the scale, and his own actions in their place, so that his own passions and self-love add nothing extra to the weight. Do that, and none of these laws of nature will fail to seem to him thoroughly reasonable.

[But in practice, only where there is security.] The laws of nature bind in foro interno — that is, within the inner court of conscience — meaning that they oblige a person to want them to be put into effect; but in foro externo — that is, in outward action — meaning actually putting them into practice, they do not always oblige. For a man who was modest and accommodating and kept every promise he made, in a place and time where no one else did the same, would only make himself a target for others and bring about his own certain ruin — which goes against the very foundation of all the laws of nature, which is the preservation of one's own nature. And likewise, a man who keeps these laws toward someone who does not keep them himself is not seeking peace but war, and is bringing about the destruction of his own nature through violence.

And whatever laws bind in foro interno can be broken not only by an act that goes against the law, but also by an act that follows the law, if the man believes it to be against the law. For even though his action in that case conforms to the law, his intention — where the obligation is in foro interno — amounts to a breach.

The laws of nature are unchanging and eternal. Injustice, ingratitude, arrogance, pride, iniquity, favoritism, and the rest can never be made lawful. For it can never be true that war preserves life while peace destroys it.

These same laws, because they oblige only to a desire and an effort — by which I mean a sincere and constant effort — are easy to observe. Since they demand nothing but effort, anyone who makes the effort to fulfill them does fulfill them; and whoever fulfills the law is just.

And the science of these laws is the one true moral philosophy. For moral philosophy is nothing but the science of what is good and evil in human conduct and society. “Good” and “evil” are names that express our desires and aversions, and these differ according to people's differing temperaments, customs, and beliefs. People differ not only in their judgments about what's pleasant or unpleasant to taste, smell, hearing, touch, and sight, but also about what agrees or conflicts with reason in the actions of everyday life. Indeed, the same person, at different times, disagrees with himself — praising, that is calling good, at one time what he condemns and calls evil at another. From this arise disputes, quarrels, and finally war. So as long as a man remains in the condition of pure nature — which is a condition of war — private appetite is the measure of good and evil. And consequently all men agree on this much: that peace is good, and therefore that the ways and means to peace — which, as I've already shown, are justice, gratitude, modesty, equity, mercy, and the rest of the laws of nature — are also good, that is, moral virtues; and their opposites are vices, which are evil. Now the science of virtue and vice is moral philosophy, and so the true doctrine of the laws of nature is the true moral philosophy. But the writers on moral philosophy, although they recognize the same virtues and vices, don't see what actually makes them good — that they come to be praised as the means to a peaceful, sociable, and comfortable life — and instead locate them in a moderate middle ground between passions, as if it were the degree of daring, not its cause, that made courage; or the size of a gift, not its motive, that made generosity.

People commonly call these dictates of reason “laws,” but that's not strictly accurate. They are really only conclusions, or theorems, about what contributes to people's self-preservation and self-defense — whereas a law, properly speaking, is the command of someone who by right has authority over others. And yet, if we think of these same theorems as delivered in the word of God, who by right commands all things, then they can properly be called laws.
